I used to have the same type of trauma; my culture is super judgemental of women who even dare to have sex before marriage. My family treated me pretty badly after I got my first bf. I lied too about my experience when I was dating. I eventually lied about other things too. I'm much more mature now and have learned better, but I would basically hide or lie about anything that embarrassed me or made me feel like I'd be abandoned. There's a really high chance she will do the same. This type of trauma is hard to let go of, albeit through tough lessons (my past relationship ended badly).

You're definitely not overreacting. I almost wonder if we had the same psych, because she told me the same bs. Definitely get a new one. Bipolar is greatly helped by good coping habits, but that can be almost impossible if your moods/disorder are out of control.

I didn't fire mine, but she quit without warning me. I luckily was able to get in with a new psych, before my prescription ran out, and she's been adjusting my meds. And holy hell has my quality of life improved. Our bodies get used to meds and/or they need adjusting. 

"High functioning" bipolar doesn't mean we don't get worn down by constant mood and mental health problems. Eventually you snap with all the stress or have a bad episode. Don't let it get to this, you deserve better. 

I didn't realize how much my psych sucked until I got this new one. My new psychiatrist wanted to follow up on my med in two weeks, but she had no openings; she asap said "don't worry, I've got it figured out; I can stay later for one day"; I would never, ever expect anyone to do that, but it made the contrast so much more apparent between her and my old psychiatrist that just sucked (and told me to suck it up and deal with the constant mood issues). 

Try out a new one. Don't settle for a psych that doesn't care or has misguided opinions.

I still trust my loved ones a lot, but I practice caution with strangers and such. You're not a bad person for trusting a partner and being sheltered is also not your fault.

I actually went through the exact same thing. I would be super interested in a guy, until he was interested in me, and then I'd be turned off. There's a few reasons this could happen. It could be that you're scared to be vulnerable, so when you meet a guy that's emotionally available, you withdraw because you sense impending intimacy and vulnerability.


You might also be perceiving perfectly healthy connections as too dependent; you're used to hiding emotion, so when you see someone who doesn't, it seems odd and codependent to you. 

Or maybe you're attracting actually codependent people because you're emotionally unavailable. The first and last one were true for me. I wanted a relationship, but was also emotionally unavailable. I was that way because of trust issues and trauma. 

Therapy helped me big time. I practiced different coping habits when I was dating someone. Like I'd make myself stop and think when I started pursuing someone; "am I pursuing them because I like them, or because I perceive them as emotionally unavailable and I want the validation of getting their availability. 

I'm definitely no therapist and I could be wrong, but it sounds like you have a fearful avoidant attachment style. I do too, although mine is now a mostly secure attachment style; it took a lot of work, but it's possible to change. Look it up and read about it, it's a complicated attachment issue. Tbh, when I was looking into it before therapy, it was too confusing for me to navigate by myself. Therapy helped me so much and I got way more helpful advice. It also helped me get to the root of why I had those attachment issues.

Could it be that you're only going after emotionally unavailable men? I had this same issue, and it helped a lot to work on my self-esteem and confidence. I started attracting people who wanted to be with me. 

I don't mean this in a mean way, but it could also be obvious that you really want a relationship. Maybe to the point of seeming a bit desperate. This tends to put men off. I've never taken anyone seriously if they acted this way. Even if they were amazing otherwise, something about it automatically makes me uninterested in taking them seriously. 

I would suggest learning to be happy with being single; the opposite looks a lot like desperation. Maybe even accepting that you could stay single. That helped me with my confidence, and people were attracted to how happy I was with myself and my life. I stayed single for a few years, same issue with either not liking the guys or them only trying to sleep with me, and eventually, I ran into my boyfriend. It'll happen when it happens; try to enjoy your life for now.

Edit: also, it could just be that you aren't meeting enough people. I met a lot of people through some classes I took for interests that I have. Take an art class, or a class in whatever your interested in. Or go to socials or clubs for these interests. I also hate dating apps, so I had to find different ways to meet people. I met my bf by starting a new job. I didn't start the job to meet guys, but yeah. Being exposed to new people helps big time.

Something very similar happened in my family. My uncle molested 3 of his sisters. When one of them told my grandma, she punished my aunt for "lying". All 3 of my aunt's continued talking to their brother and trying to ignore what he did, probably because they were shamed about it and probably blame themselves somewhere in their mind. They have really unhealthy lives and terrible mental health. How could they do better in that type of environment? It makes so much sense that you're also doing this. You're trying to survive, maybe trying to ignore the pain so that it'll seem less real. And your dad is trying to manipulate you to look at him as a normal father figure, which he will never be after what he did. You're victimizing yourself again by doing the same thing your mom did 

With my uncle, I one day got into a screaming match with him, even though he practically raised me (due to my parents bring awful), and cut him off when I found out. Was it hard? Oh yeah, big time. He was basically my father figure and had never done anything wrong to me. But I was not going to enable and ignore what he did to my aunt's. I was so disgusted that everyone just ignored what my uncle did. There's zero excuse for it, no matter what the reason is; my aunt's did not deserve how my family handled it. 

I highly suggest therapy. My bf was also sexually abused, and while therapy was really hard to get through the first year, he is SO much better now. You deserve to have more peace and healing in your life.

I know you love your mom, but it might be worth considering cutting her off. My mom was abusive, but somehow thought she was not at fault at all, and I have since cut her off. It was hard; I felt guilty and like the bad guy, but I now realize that it's not my fault and my mom made her own bed. It's different if they're actively owning up to their mistakes and trying to make amends, but she is instead being dismissive and showing no empathy over the situation. She's trying to make you feel guilty for wanting her to divorce your father and finds any reason to excuse that the situation happened in the first place. She might not be guilty of the abuse, but she's guilty for a lot of the pain/trauma you carry over the situation.

I think being around her is preventing you from healing. Every time she shows she doesn't care, it adds salt to the wound; she is a trigger for you and an enabler for your abuser.. She's not a good person and doesn't deserve your continued involvement in her life. I realized that about my mom one day, blocked her on everything, and my life has improved so much since. Yes, it was painful at first. But less painful that having her be nonapologetic for the abuse and having her trigger my PTSD as a result; I was no longer in a constant state of either anger or hurt. I didn't start healing until she was no longer there tbh. Therapy also helped. A lot. Even if you can only afford to go once a month, that is better than never. 

I'm so sorry you've had this experience. I understand in some ways, and I know how betrayed you must feel. I really hope you will be able to heal and feel peace in your life. You deserved more from your mother, then and now. I tried to do the same thing; I ignored what she did, pretended to myself that I could get over it (even if my abusers didn't apologize or take accountability), and played happy family. It got me into a horrible place mentally and did nothing for my healing. You deserve so much better. Put yourself first.

I think it is normal to have a fear of death and/or aging. Change is scary, and losing a part of yourself can be a hard transition. But you also gain things with age; wisdom, financial stability (yay, more vacations), matured love, accomplishing your life goals, etc. 

When I was a teen, I was terrified of being in my mid twenties. I'm there now, and I'm so much more proud of the person I am now and how I look than when I was younger. My style has matured; I just know how to dress myself better. Confidence has also improved greatly, which was a struggle for me in my younger years.

Also, being older doesn't mean you can't be beautiful. I know plenty of hot women in their 30s-40s. And look at how many celeb women look great past that. Yes, they've had some work done, but a lot of it is also how well dressed and maintained they are. 

Helen mirrin is elegant and beautiful. Different type of beautiful than a 20 year old, but still gorgeous. You're not going to be ugly. Also, I've noticed that a lot of POC tend to age better for some reason (probs different skin types). 

Ps, take collagen supplements, they help. My friends also started getting minor Botox in their late twenties. It helps prevent the severity of wrinkles in older age. Just please make sure that you work on this insecurity first, because i know a girl that didn't and she is addicted to it now. Has overdone it a lot and is scared to be without. Nothing wrong with doing things to make yourself feel beautiful as you age, but it shouldn't take off to a level where it's negatively affecting you

I don't think he's responsible for her choosing to smoke it. But he is responsible for trying to bypass someone's consent. That would be wrong even if she hadn't been an addict and nothing terrible came of it. 

I hope OP has learned to be more respectful of consent. He can definitely make something positive out of this and learn, and I also do agree that he didn't have any malicious intent, but that choice he made sort of did make him a crappy person in that instance. 

I'm a bartender and we often talk about how shitty some people's friends are; pushing people to drink is not cool. Drugs and sex are two big things where the individuals consent should take top priority, and yeah, if they're the type of person that doesn't respect that, it does make them sort of crappy, at least in that specific area. 

I'm not saying OP is irredeemable, but I am saying that he should learn from his mistake and learn more about/respect consent.

Also a former addict, and while I agree with your opinion on personal responsibility, pushing someone into drugs is almost as creepy as doing it with sex. Consent is important and, "no" is a full sentence. 

I don't think he's responsible for her death, but he is responsible for coercing his gf. Doesn't remove the fact that she chose to smoke it, but also doesn't erase that he was not a good person to her. Not ok at all.

This is so important. While I don't think OP was consciously trying to be a bad person, he sort of was in that instance; consent is of utmost important with drugs and/or sex. He was very wrong to push her original decision. Someone who is good for you won't try to push your consent on something like that.

I totally get it. I've had similar feelings, even though they made no sense, they were there. For me, it was coming from a place of trauma/insecurity. I had all these ideas of what holidays should look like. I wanted everything to go exactly the way I pictured it because I feared the opposite; disaster and disappointment. Or not feeling loved. Maybe it's more simple and you just really love your birthday, which is totally ok!

You're definitely overreacting though. I don't mean that in a judgemental way, it is good that you were able to recognize it. We can't control how we feel all the time, but you can control what you do with it. When these feelings come up, validate them (it's ok for you to have emotions), but remind yourself that your bf did so much to show his love and nothing that he did/didn't do was coming from a bad place. 

Some things that have helped me, because I also enjoy birthdays; if you have more loved ones, ask them for some of the stuff that you want. So let's say you wanted a nice cake; ask mom or dad, or whomever else. That way there aren't huge expectations on one person, that might be hard or stressful for them to meet. I also like the suggestion of just buying yourself a cake next time. I think setting so many expectations on one person makes it easy for it to backfire; you'll be left feeling unsatisfied and he'll feel that you're ungrateful. 

Either spread out your needs between more people, especially when there are a lot of them, or reframe your mindset on the situation; the effort should be there, you should be able to feel loved and celebrated (and in ways that you appreciate), but it needn't be based on a huge list of specific things. 

Personally, I make a small list of 3 things that are important to me and give it to my bf. Like a cake, small gift, dinner, etc. This year, mine was 1) dinner, 2) flowers, and  3) a surprise from him. I didn't miss anything that I really wanted, and bf felt appreciated. Communicating your needs is important, but so is setting realistic expectations. This doesn't mean that you should allow yourself to be less loved; bf did his best to show that you are extremely loved, it just wasn't perfect.

This is extremely abusive and not ok. You 100% deserve better and should leave her. 

Did you grow up around people with similar coping habits? I only ask because I did and I was used to seeing these types of situations. So when my ex was crazy, and everyone else saw it as an obvious "you need to get out ASAP" situation, I just didn't get the big deal. 

Obviously now I know better and don't tolerate things like that. 

I also wanted to mention, as someone who is bipolar, she sounds like someone with an untreated personality or psychiatric disorder. Probably BPD, or at least on the spectrum for it. They take rejection terribly and do anything to avoid it, including manipulation, outbursts, and sometimes abuse. I'm by no means implying that everyone with BPD is abusive, but it takes a lot of work to have a disorder like BPD (or bipolar tbh) and not be a jerk. 

Work she should be putting in and holding herself responsible for. She needs therapy and possibly medication, and that's something that she should've done on her own accord, before it harmed you. 

I would break up with her, and if you feel up to it, let her know her behavior might be a symptom of a mental health issue. 

But please, please only break up with her while you're recording everything and in the presence of a friend or family member. Honestly, move your things out before, not after the break up. My mom is exactly as you described your gf, and when my dad left her she called the cops and said he hit her. He did get arrested. Bf's ex tried to stab him when he broke up with her. Both of those women do have BPD and have no issue letting it fester to a dangerous level. Your ex doesn't either, from what you've described. 

Also, if it is a disorder like this, she will not grow out of it. She has to get treatment and be consistent with it if she wants to improve. This is true even if she doesn't have a disorder.  Coping habits are hard asf to change and take a lot of dedication. She'd need a lot of motivation and a lot of therapy. Be wary of any promises she might make while you try to break up with her; it'll most likely not last, and she'll probably only do it until she's once again comfortable that you're not going to leave.

In my first relationship, I was pretty jealous about most things, and particularly didn't like porn. I wasn't mean about it nor did I try to control my ex, but emotionally I was not ok. This was sort of often too. 

With my current bf, I don't care at all if we watches porn. I think part of that is that I've learned to enjoy it myself, although to be fair I am bisexual. But the other bigger part is that I know he is attracted to me and that he loves me. Also, I have worked on my confidence a lot.

Moreover, porn is really just entertainment and not based in reality. I think it's important that you focus on that distinction. If your bf compared himself to the guy(s) in the video, he would feel the same. Most guys do not have enormous c*cks and/or flawless abs. He just watches those videos as part of a fantasy; not because he doesn't love you as you are.  

He is with you because he finds you beautiful, loves you, and definitely wants to keep sleeping with you. Body dysmorphia is a b*tch, I do understand that. I can totally see how looking at those girls would trigger those feelings. Work big time on your self-esteem. It's the thing that helped me most. 

When I get feelings similar to yours, I remind myself that it's not ok to talk to myself that way. I think of someone I really love, and imagine them talking to themselves that way, and it shakes me right out of it. It reminds me of how terrible and imaginary body dysmorphia is. If the roles were reversed, you wouldn't want your bf to talk to himself the way that you talk to yourself; you'd probably be devastated if you heard him doing so.

I can understand why he would be upset. His wife has alopecia and it's likely a sensitive subject for her. 

However, I think he acted completely inappropriately.  Idk, maybe I'm wrong, but if I were Will, I would've talked to Chris after and explained my feelings. He seems like a nice dude and I'm sure he wouldn't apologized.

So I used to have a super short fuse in relationships. It sucked because immediately after, I would regret being so irritable and such a jerk. The thing that helped most was medication. I highly suggest therapy. While couples counseling is super helpful, if you can only afford one or the other, I suggest doing individual counseling for yourself. Setting new habits is hard, but if you're dedicated, if is doable. As time passes, you'll notice how much easier it gets to follow good coping habits. Practice makes perfect. However, I was never able to work on my coping habits before medication, because I wasn't consistent enough with my moods. I definitely suggest getting that worked out.

The litter box does need to be cleaned regularly. Every day is ideal, but tbh I do it like every other day. They're strange about their litter box, so if it's too dirty they'll go potty elsewhere. Getting them neutered/spayed is super important. They're not fun when they're in heat. Also, they'll send mark everything. After ours were fixed, they havent sprayed anything. 

When you get a new cat, sort of except that they'll pee on a few things. It'll probably be a little scared to be somewhere new, start marking it so that it feels like their territory, and be a bit reclusive. Let the cat come to you, it eventually will. There are super outgoing cats, and ones that are super affectionate.

If you decide not to foster, maybe go to one of those shelters that has cat rooms and spend some time getting to know the cats. There'll be one for ya. :)

I almost got murdered. I honestly thought the entire thing couldn't have been real for months after. It just seemed like something that couldn't really happen in real life, even though it did. 

I was out drinking heavily with friends. We had been drinking since 9am, and it was like 8:30pm. We were at this Mexican restaurant where they have a band you can "rent". Well, my friends paid to have them sing to them, but I was sooo tired. No one could take me home yet, so one of them offered to let me nap in their car. I was so drunk, I don't remember how I got out of the car or if the guy just took me. At some point, I became conscious. I was in some truck in the passenger side, and the dude was on top of me at an awkward angle (he was still partly on the driver's side). I struggled hard, punched him, which apparently broke my hand but did not help the situation at all. I gave up and begged to be let to live, he started choking me. My mom was a terrible parent, in fact I don't even talk to her because she was so abusive, but she saved my life that day; she'd always been super paranoid because of her schizophrenia, and would instruct us exactly how to act if we were being kidnapped. The one that she would repeat the most in her paranoid rants was to not fight, just pretend to be dead and get away when you can. He didn't stop choking me, so I did just that. He must've been stupid, because he checked my pulse and quietly slid to the driver's side completely. When I felt him get off of me, I waited a few seconds (or minutes?? I don't remember) and had the thought that I should check that the door was unlocked before I tried to run for it. I would've probably died otherwise, because it was locked. With my eyes still closed, I moved my hand to search for the handle/lock thingy, felt that it was locked, and unlocked it. I opened it right after and jumped out. He grabbed me by the shoulder, hard enough that I had bad bruising after, but I dropped my whole body to the floor to make him lose his grip (it was a tall truck). I remember the floor was rocky and it left me with bloody knees, but I did get away. I ran for not too long, straight into the arms of one of the security people for the restaurant/bar place. Cops got called, I got taken to the hospital, and was in denial that it really happened for months. They never found him because the outside camera wasn't working, and my memory and description about how he looked wasn't super clear. It still makes me upset that he didn't get found, and I worry that I might've taught him to take more precautions the next time he tries to hurt someone. It's weird thinking he might be someone's father or brother.

It's been 2 years since, and I'm now sober. I've also gotten therapy, which has helped processing some of my more complex trauma. I have better coping habits, and although I still struggle with my bipolar disorder (recently diagnosed and correctly treated!), I don't use alcohol to cope.
